explanations.answer: By what authority He does these things
explanations.explanation: They ask Him, “By what authority are You doing these things?” and then add, “And who gave You the authority to do them?” (Mark 11:28). That's two questions stacked in one breath. Hold onto your apron, because Jesus is about to turn the conversation around.

explanations.answer: Why His disciples don't fast like others
explanations.explanation: That one isn't what they ask here. In this passage they ask, “By what authority are You doing these things?” (Mark 11:28). They're asking about what Jesus has been doing, and who gave Him the right to do it. Fasting never comes up in this scene.

explanations.answer: Which commandment matters most of all
explanations.explanation: Good question, friend, but nobody asks it in this scene. The chief priests, scribes and elders say, “By what authority are You doing these things?” (Mark 11:28). They want to know about His authority. Keep your eye on that word, because it drives the whole passage.

explanations.answer: Tell them by what authority He acts
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “…and if you answer Me, I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.” (Mark 11:29). So He sets up a trade: their answer first, His answer after. Notice He doesn't dodge them. He just picks the order.

explanations.answer: Leave the temple courts for good
explanations.explanation: Jesus never says anything about leaving. He's walking in the temple courts when they come up to Him (Mark 11:27), and He stays right there to talk. His offer is this: “…if you answer Me, I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.” (Mark 11:29).

The disciples don't get pulled into this one. Jesus says, “…if you answer Me, I will tell you by what authority I am doing these things.” (Mark 11:29). The promise is about telling them His authority, and nothing else is on the table.

Jesus asks about John, the one who baptized people, and puts it this way: “…was it from heaven or from men?” (Mark 11:30). Two choices, no third door. I think that's why this question feels like a tight squeeze.
Moses and Elijah aren't in this question at all. Jesus asks whether John's baptism was “…from heaven or from men?” (Mark 11:30). Those are the only two options He puts out there.
Countries don't come up here, friend. Jesus asks, “…was it from heaven or from men?” (Mark 11:30). It's about where John's baptism came from, and He gives exactly two choices.

They say it themselves: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’” (Mark 11:31). They can see the trap closing before they step in it. I've talked myself out of a dozen bad ideas that way, usually in the cookie aisle of my own head.

explanations.answer: Why they let John be arrested
explanations.explanation: Nothing about an arrest comes up in their huddle. They say, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’” (Mark 11:31). Their worry is about not believing John.

explanations.answer: Why they never went to see John
explanations.explanation: That's not what they're afraid of being asked. Their words are, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ He will ask, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’” (Mark 11:31). The question on their minds is about belief, plain and simple.

Roman soldiers don't show up anywhere in this scene, friend. The text says, “…they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John truly was a prophet.” (Mark 11:32). So the crowd is what worries the leaders, not soldiers.

That's right, there are no soldiers here. The text says, “…they were afraid of the people, for they all held that John truly was a prophet.” (Mark 11:32). The crowd's opinion of John is what boxes the leaders in.
They answer, “We do not know.” (Mark 11:33). They had two doors and chose to say neither. Honestly, I've used that move on a smoke alarm at 2 a.m., and it never helped me either.

They don't say that, because they'd already worked out what would come next: “Why then did you not believe him?” (Mark 11:31). So they steer clear of it. What they actually say is, “We do not know.” (Mark 11:33).
They don't say that either. They were “afraid of the people, for they all held that John truly was a prophet.” (Mark 11:32). So they land on, “We do not know.” (Mark 11:33).

Jesus holds to the deal He made. He replies, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.” (Mark 11:33). No answer from them, no answer from Him. It's a fair trade, and they're the ones who left it empty.

The text says the opposite. After they say, “We do not know,” Jesus replies, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.” (Mark 11:33). He told them the terms back in verse 29, and He keeps to them.

explanations.answer: Rents it to tenants and goes on a journey
explanations.explanation: Jesus says the man “rented it out to some tenants and went away on a journey.” (Mark 12:1). So the owner steps back and trusts others to work his land. Remember who's in that vineyard, because it matters soon.

explanations.answer: Sells it to a neighbor and stays close by
explanations.explanation: No sale happens in this parable. Jesus says the man “rented it out to some tenants and went away on a journey.” (Mark 12:1). He rents it out, and he travels away.

explanations.answer: Keeps it himself and works the land
explanations.explanation: The owner doesn't work it himself. Jesus says he “rented it out to some tenants and went away on a journey.” (Mark 12:1). The tenants are the ones on the land.

explanations.answer: Beat him and send him away empty-handed
explanations.explanation: Jesus says, “But they seized the servant, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed.” (Mark 12:3). The servant came for the owner's share and left with nothing. That's a hard turn in the story.

explanations.answer: Pay him and send him home with thanks
explanations.explanation: Nobody pays anybody here. Jesus says, “But they seized the servant, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed.” (Mark 12:3). The servant leaves with nothing.

explanations.answer: Tell him to wait for the next harvest
explanations.explanation: They don't ask him to wait. Jesus says, “But they seized the servant, beat him, and sent him away empty-handed.” (Mark 12:3). It's a rough welcome for someone just doing the owner's errand.

The owner keeps going. Jesus says, “He sent still another, and this one they killed. He sent many others; some they beat and others they killed.” (Mark 12:5). So he doesn't stop after the second servant. The story is heavy here, and it stays heavy for a bit.

Right, he doesn't stop. Jesus says, “He sent still another, and this one they killed. He sent many others; some they beat and others they killed.” (Mark 12:5). It's a heavy part of the story, so I'll say that once and keep moving.
Jesus says, “Finally, having one beloved son, he sent him to them.” (Mark 12:6). The word “one” stands out to me. After all those servants, this is the last one the owner sends in the story.
A steward isn't in this parable. Jesus says, “Finally, having one beloved son, he sent him to them.” (Mark 12:6). The last one sent is family.
No cupbearer shows up in this story, friend. Jesus says, “Finally, having one beloved son, he sent him to them.” (Mark 12:6). The one he sends is his son.
The owner says, “They will respect my son.” (Mark 12:6). He sends his son expecting a better welcome than the servants got. I think that hope is what makes the next verse hit so hard.
Paying double isn't what he's hoping for. The owner says, “They will respect my son.” (Mark 12:6). It's respect he expects, not money.
Hiding isn't in the owner's expectations. He says, “They will respect my son.” (Mark 12:6). He sends his son and expects respect.

The tenants say, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” (Mark 12:7). They know exactly who he is. It's a dark plan, so I'll just say that plainly and leave it there.
Rent isn't what they name. They say, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” (Mark 12:7). They're after the inheritance.
The harvest isn't their stated goal. They say, “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.” (Mark 12:7). It's the inheritance they're after.

Jesus says, “So they seized the son, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.” (Mark 12:8). The vineyard is the same place the owner planted and walled in at the start. It's a heavy moment in the parable.

The watchtower is in the story, because the owner built one (Mark 12:1). But it isn't where the son is thrown. Jesus says, “So they seized the son, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.” (Mark 12:8).
No city is named in this part of the parable. Jesus says, “So they seized the son, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard.” (Mark 12:8). The vineyard is the setting the whole way through.

explanations.answer: Kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others
explanations.explanation: Jesus answers it Himself: “He will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” (Mark 12:9). It's a hard line, and the passage doesn't soften it. The vineyard goes to others.

explanations.answer: Forgive those tenants and let them keep farming
explanations.explanation: That isn't how Jesus answers His own question. He says, “He will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” (Mark 12:9). The vineyard doesn't stay with these tenants.

explanations.answer: Sell the vineyard and never come back again
explanations.explanation: No sale in this answer, friend. Jesus says, “He will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.” (Mark 12:9). The owner comes, and he gives the vineyard to others.

Jesus quotes, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” (Mark 12:10). The builders tossed it aside, and it became the most important stone. I've been set aside in a drawer myself, so I like this verse more than most.
A memorial stone isn't what the verse says. Jesus quotes, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” (Mark 12:10). It's a building stone, and it takes the key spot.
The verse doesn't use a boundary stone. Jesus quotes, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” (Mark 12:10). The rejected stone ends up as the cornerstone.

The Scripture says, “This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” (Mark 12:11). So the stone's new place comes from the Lord, and the people looking on find it marvelous. That's the end of what Jesus quotes.

The Scripture says the opposite of False. It says, “This is from the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” (Mark 12:11). The stone's new place is from the Lord, and it's marvelous to those who see it.
The text says, “…they knew that He had spoken this parable against them.” (Mark 12:12). They don't need a map to see where it points. Some stories land so close to home you could mail them there.
No governor appears in this scene. The text says, “…they knew that He had spoken this parable against them.” (Mark 12:12). The “them” is the leaders who came up to Jesus.

The money changers aren't in this scene. The text says the leaders “knew that He had spoken this parable against them.” (Mark 12:12). The ones who knew it was aimed at them are the leaders themselves.

The text says, “But fearing the crowd, they left Him and went away.” (Mark 12:12). The same crowd that boxed them in about John is boxing them in again. Some things don't change by the end of the day.
The disciples aren't mentioned as guards here. The text says, “But fearing the crowd, they left Him and went away.” (Mark 12:12). The crowd is what holds them back.
No temple guards appear in this verse. The text says, “But fearing the crowd, they left Him and went away.” (Mark 12:12). Fear of the crowd is what stops them. This story isn't over, friend.
